127.title: Sukkot: the booth
127.hook: a flimsy hut with a leafy roof, where people eat for a week under the stars
127.howItsDone: During Sukkot, many Jewish families build a sukkah with a roof of cut branches or reeds and eat their meals in it for seven days, some sleeping there too. Some welcome the ushpizin, biblical guests, along with real ones.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Neilah: the last prayer of Yom Kippur, as the gates close. Your line was before the gates close. Did you say your sentence? Five days after the fast, the mood flips completely. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

Walk down certain streets in the fall and you'll see them: little huts on balconies, in backyards, in parking lots, even on apartment rooftops. Walls of canvas or plywood. A roof of palm fronds, bamboo mats or branches, with gaps you can see through. Paper chains and hanging fruit. A folding table inside, and a family eating dinner in their coats. Some people even sleep out there. Many families start building on the night Yom Kippur ends, still tasting the first meal after the fast. For a week, the fanciest room in the house is a shack.
screen: `HUTS ON BALCONIES AND ROOFTOPS.` → `A ROOF OF BRANCHES.` → `DINNER IN YOUR COAT.`

segments.voice: The hut is a sukkah, and the holiday is Sukkot, the plural: booths. It begins on the fifteenth of the month, under the full moon, and lasts seven days. The Torah says: "Ye shall dwell in booths seven days," so that each generation would remember that the Israelites lived in booths when they came out of Egypt. It's also a harvest festival, the last gathering of the year before the rains, and the Torah calls it a time to rejoice. The rabbis call it the season of our joy. The rules are what make it beautiful. A sukkah needs at least three walls, though the Talmud allows less. It has to be temporary. And the roof must be made of things that grew from the ground and have been cut, like branches or reeds, laid loosely enough that the stars can be seen through them at night, but thick enough that there's more shade than sun by day. So right after the most serious day of the year, Jews move out of their solid homes and into something fragile. Why? One answer: to remember that everything we build is more temporary than it looks, and that people once lived under God's protection with nothing but branches overhead. There's a lovely custom too. Each night, some families welcome ushpizin, guests: Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, Aaron, Joseph and David, and in many homes the women of the Bible as well, and they invite real guests to share the meal. And if it pours? The Mishnah says go inside. The sukkah is for joy, not misery.
screen: `SUKKOT: SEVEN DAYS IN BOOTHS.` · `A ROOF YOU CAN SEE STARS THROUGH.` · `A FRAGILE HOUSE ON PURPOSE.` · `GUESTS, AND GO IN IF IT RAINS.` · then, large: `YE SHALL DWELL IN BOOTHS SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat one meal outside. A porch, a park bench, a step. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture a roof of loose branches above you, with the sky showing through. Think about what in your life is sturdier than it looks, and what's more fragile than it looks. A job, a body, a friendship. Hold both kinds lightly for a minute. If you pray, you might give thanks for shelter. The bell holds the time.
Sukkah. A booth: a temporary hut with a roof of branches, where Jews eat, and some sleep, for the seven days of Sukkot.
Your line: live lightly for a week. Today, eat under the open sky if you can, and notice how little a good meal really needs. Day one hundred twenty-seven.

128.title: Sukkot: the four kinds (Leviticus 23:40)
128.hook: palm, myrtle, willow and citron, which midrash reads as four kinds of people held together
128.howItsDone: On each day of Sukkot except Shabbat, many Jews hold the lulav, myrtle and willow together with the etrog, say a blessing, and wave them in six directions, and carry them around the synagogue during the Hoshanot prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sukkah: a fragile hut with a roof of branches and stars. Your line was live lightly for a week. Did you eat outside? Today, what people hold in their hands in that hut. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

On a Sukkot morning, you might see someone standing in a sukkah holding what looks like a strange bouquet. In the right hand, a tall, closed palm branch, bound together with sprigs of green leaves. In the left hand, a yellow fruit that looks like a bumpy lemon, held so carefully you'd think it was made of glass. People pay real money for a perfect one. They say a blessing, bring both hands together, and then begin to wave the whole bundle: forward, to the side, behind, up, down. Shaking gently, so the leaves rustle.
screen: `A STRANGE BOUQUET.` → `A LEMON HELD LIKE GLASS.` → `WAVED IN EVERY DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: It all comes from one verse. The Torah says that on the first day of the festival, "ye shall take you on the first day the fruit of goodly trees, branches of palm-trees, and boughs of thick trees, and willows of the brook," and rejoice. The rabbis identified the four: the etrog, a citron, for the goodly fruit; the lulav, a young palm branch; hadasim, myrtle, whose leaves grow thick and overlapping; and aravot, willows that grow by water. The whole bundle is often just called the lulav, after the tallest piece. Then the midrash asks a beautiful question: why these four? And it answers by taste and smell. The etrog has both a taste and a fragrance, like people who have both learning and good deeds. The palm's fruit, the date, has taste but no smell: learning without deeds. The myrtle has a lovely smell but no taste: good deeds without learning. And the willow has neither. What does God do with the willows, the midrash asks? Throw them away? No. Bind them all together into one bundle, and each one makes up for the others. You can't do this mitzvah with three of the four. Leave out the plain willow and the whole thing doesn't count. Then the waving. Many wave toward all six directions, east, south, west, north, up and down, a way of saying that God is everywhere and that blessing can come from any side. The rabbis also linked it to the coming rains; Sukkot sits right before the rainy season, and the willows, the plants that need water most, are part of the prayer.
screen: `FOUR KINDS FROM ONE VERSE.` · `TASTE, SMELL, BOTH, OR NEITHER.` · `ALL FOUR, OR IT DOESN'T COUNT.` · `WAVED TOWARD SIX DIRECTIONS.` · then, large: `WILLOWS OF THE BROOK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: point slowly to six directions. Settle, and breathe. Point ahead of you, and think of someone in front of you in life, someone you look up to. Point to one side, then the other, and think of the people beside you. Point behind you: the people who came before. Point up. Point down, to the ground that holds you. Then bring your hands together, and think of one person who feels like a willow, easy to leave out. Hold them in the bundle. The bell holds the time.
Lulav. A young palm branch, bound with myrtle and willow and held with the etrog: four kinds of plants, and four kinds of people, together.
Your line: every kind together. Today, include one person you'd usually leave out: the quiet one, the difficult one, the one who doesn't fit. Day one hundred twenty-eight.

129.title: Simchat Torah
129.hook: the reading finishes Deuteronomy and begins Genesis on the same day, with dancing
129.carry: finish and begin the same day
129.howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, synagogues take out all their Torah scrolls and dance with them in seven circuits called hakafot, read the end of Deuteronomy and the start of Genesis, and in many places call all the children up together under a prayer shawl.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lulav: palm, myrtle, willow and citron, bound together. Your line was every kind together. Who did you bring into the bundle? Day one hundred twenty-nine.

Picture the most serious room you know, a place of quiet prayer, and now picture it at its loudest. Every Torah scroll has been taken out of the ark. People are carrying them in their arms like partners at a wedding, dancing in circles around the room, singing, sometimes spilling out into the street. Kids ride on shoulders waving flags. Someone's grandfather, who never dances, is dancing. A scroll gets passed to someone who's never held one before. The circles go around seven times, and nobody's in a hurry. This is the last day of the fall holidays.
screen: `EVERY SCROLL OUT OF THE ARK.` → `DANCING WITH THE TORAH.` → `SEVEN TIMES AROUND.`

segments.voice: The day is called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah. It comes right after Sukkot. In Israel it's the same day as the festival called Shemini Atzeret; outside Israel it's the day after. Here's why everyone's dancing. All year long, week by week, synagogues read the Five Books of Moses in order, one portion each Shabbat. On Simchat Torah, that yearly reading ends. Someone is called up to read the very last lines of Deuteronomy, where Moses dies and the Torah closes with the words "in the sight of all Israel." And then, right away, with no break, a second scroll is opened and someone else reads the first lines of Genesis: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." The two people called up are given honorary titles, the bridegroom of the Torah and the bridegroom of Genesis, and in many communities today, brides too. Why start again immediately? So that no one could say the Jews finished the Torah and were done with it. The circle never closes; it just turns. There's a lovely detail rabbis like to point out. The last letter of the Torah is lamed, from the word Israel. The first letter is bet, from the word bereshit, in the beginning. Put the end and the beginning together, lamed and bet, and you get lev: heart. And one more: on this day, in many synagogues, all the children are called up together under one big prayer shawl, spread over them like a canopy. Nobody is too young. The joy is in holding the book, not in having mastered it.
screen: `SIMCHAT TORAH: THE JOY OF THE TORAH.` · `THE LAST LINES OF DEUTERONOMY.` · `THEN, AT ONCE, GENESIS.` · `END AND BEGINNING SPELL HEART.` · then, large: `IN THE BEGINNING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: reread the first line of something you love. A book, a song, a poem, a letter someone wrote you. Before you do, settle, and breathe. Think of something you've finished recently: a project, a season, a chapter of your life. Let it be finished. Then ask what might begin right now, today, not someday. Hold the end and the beginning in the same breath. The bell holds the time.
Simchat Torah. The joy of the Torah: the day the year's reading ends with Deuteronomy and begins again with Genesis, with dancing.
Your line: finish and begin the same day. Today, when you finish something, start the next thing before you walk away, even just the first line. Day one hundred twenty-nine.

130.title: Hanukkah: the lights
130.hook: a small revolt, a rededicated Temple, and eight nights of lights in the window
130.howItsDone: For eight nights from the 25th of Kislev, Jewish families light a hanukkiah, adding one light each night with the shamash, say blessings, and place it in a window or doorway where passersby can see it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simchat Torah: dancing with the scrolls, ending Deuteronomy and beginning Genesis. Your line was finish and begin the same day. Now we jump ahead two months, to the darkest nights of the year. Day one hundred thirty.

Drive through certain neighborhoods on a December night and look at the windows. In some of them, a row of small flames: two, three, maybe eight, with one standing a little higher or off to the side. Sometimes they're candles in a silver holder, sometimes little cups of olive oil, sometimes a child's clay creation. They're not hidden in the dining room. They're placed in the window, facing the street, on purpose. Whoever lit them wants you, a stranger driving by, to see them. That's part of the point.
screen: `A ROW OF SMALL FLAMES.` → `PLACED IN THE WINDOW.` → `MEANT FOR STRANGERS TO SEE.`

segments.voice: Hanukkah means dedication. The story is about two thousand two hundred years old. The land of Israel was ruled by a Greek-speaking kingdom, and its king, Antiochus the Fourth, outlawed Jewish practice: Shabbat, circumcision, Torah study. The Temple in Jerusalem was turned over to the worship of other gods. A priestly family, led by an old man named Mattathias and then his son Judah, called the Maccabee, led a small revolt. Against the odds, they won back Jerusalem, cleaned the Temple, and rededicated it, on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev. That's the history, told in the books of the Maccabees. Those books aren't in the Hebrew Bible, which is why Hanukkah is a festival set by the rabbis, not by the Torah. Then the Talmud adds the part most people know. When the Temple was retaken, there was only one small jar of pure oil left, enough to light the Temple menorah for one day. It burned for eight. So Hanukkah lasts eight nights. And the Talmud gives the lights a job: they are meant to publicize the miracle. That's why they go in a doorway or a window facing the street, and why they're lit when people are still out walking. The lamp itself is often called a hanukkiah: eight lights, plus a helper light, the shamash, used to light the others. Hanukkah is not one of the major holidays in Jewish law; work goes on as normal. But it may be the most visible one. For a people who were once told not to be seen practicing, the whole mitzvah is to be seen.
screen: `HANUKKAH: DEDICATION.` · `A SMALL REVOLT, A CLEANED TEMPLE.` · `ONE JAR OF OIL, EIGHT NIGHTS.` · `LIGHTS IN THE WINDOW, TO BE SEEN.` · then, large: `PUBLICIZE THE MIRACLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: put a light where others can see it. A candle in the window tonight, a lamp left on for a neighbor, or something small and good you'd usually keep private. For now, settle, and breathe. Picture a single flame in a dark window. Think about what you believe in, or love, that you keep hidden because it might look strange. Just notice it. You don't have to announce anything. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. Dedication: eight nights of lights, placed in the window, remembering a rededicated Temple and a little oil that lasted.
Your line: add a light each night. Tonight, leave one light on where someone passing by can see it. Day one hundred thirty.

131.title: Hanukkah: counting up (Shabbat 21b)
131.hook: Shammai said start with eight and go down; Hillel said start with one and go up, and Jews follow Hillel
131.howItsDone: Following the House of Hillel, Jews light one Hanukkah light on the first night and add one each night until eight, lighting the newest first with the shamash.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lights of Hanukkah, placed in the window to be seen. Your line was add a light each night. But why add? Why not start with all eight? That was once a real argument. Day one hundred thirty-one.

Every family that lights Hanukkah candles does the same thing. The first night, one candle, plus the helper. The second night, two. By the eighth night, the whole row is blazing. Kids count them. It feels so natural you'd never think to question it. But about two thousand years ago, in the Talmud's telling, the two great schools of Jewish law looked at those same eight nights and disagreed completely. One said you start full and go down. The other said you start small and go up. Both had good reasons. Only one became the custom.
screen: `ONE CANDLE, THEN TWO, THEN EIGHT.` → `IT FEELS SO NATURAL.` → `ONCE, A REAL ARGUMENT.`

segments.voice: The two schools were the House of Shammai and the House of Hillel, the students of two famous teachers who lived around the time of Herod. They disagreed on hundreds of questions. This is one of the most famous. The Talmud, in tractate Shabbat, page twenty-one, lays it out. The House of Shammai said: on the first night, light eight, and each night, one fewer. The House of Hillel said: on the first night, light one, and each night, one more. Then it gives the reasons. Shammai's side said the lights should match the days still to come: eight days left, eight lights; one day left, one light. There's real sense in that. It's honest about time running out. Hillel's side gave a different kind of reason: in matters of holiness, we go up, and we don't go down. The Hebrew phrase is short, ma'alin ba-kodesh, we raise in holiness. And Jewish practice follows the House of Hillel, as it does in almost every case. The Talmud elsewhere says why Hillel's school usually won: they were kind and humble, and they taught their opponents' views, even quoting Shammai's opinion before their own. So think about what that means for a practice. Shammai's way is a countdown. It ends small. Hillel's way is a count up. It ends in the most light, on the darkest nights of the year. The question isn't just how many candles. It's which direction you want your life to be going.
screen: `THE HOUSE OF SHAMMAI: EIGHT, THEN DOWN.` · `THE HOUSE OF HILLEL: ONE, THEN UP.` · `WE RAISE IN HOLINESS.` · `THE PRACTICE FOLLOWS HILLEL.` · then, large: `ALWAYS GO UP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: add one small good thing each day. Start now, with one. Settle, and breathe. Pick something tiny: one glass of water, one kind word, one page read, one minute of quiet. Tomorrow, do it again and add a little. Not a countdown of things to give up, but a count up of things to add. Picture a single flame, and next to it, the space where tomorrow's goes. The bell holds the time.
Hanukkah. Dedication, and a count that rises: one light the first night, eight by the last, because in holiness we go up.
Your line: always go up. Today, do one small good thing, and tomorrow, do it again and add one more. Day one hundred thirty-one.

132.title: Tu BiShvat
132.hook: the new year for trees, marked with fruits of the land of Israel
132.howItsDone: On Tu BiShvat, many Jews eat fruits, especially those the Torah links to the land of Israel, some hold a Tu BiShvat seder of fruits and wine, and many plant trees or support planting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the House of Hillel's count: one light, then two, then eight. Your line was always go up. What did you add today? Now, in the middle of winter, a new year. For trees. Day one hundred thirty-two.

The Talmud tells a story about a man named Honi. He's walking along a road and sees an old man planting a carob tree. Honi asks him: how long until that tree gives fruit? Seventy years, says the old man. Honi can't believe it. Do you really think you'll be alive in seventy years to eat from it? And the old man answers, more or less: I found this world full of carob trees. My grandparents planted them for me. So I'm planting this one for my grandchildren. Honi, the story goes, then falls asleep for seventy years. When he wakes, a young man is picking carobs from that tree.
screen: `AN OLD MAN PLANTS A CAROB.` → `SEVENTY YEARS TO BEAR FRUIT.` → `PLANTED FOR THE GRANDCHILDREN.`

segments.voice: The Mishnah lists four different new years in the Jewish calendar, each for a different purpose. One of them is the new year for trees. The House of Shammai said it falls on the first of the month of Shevat; the House of Hillel said the fifteenth, and once again, Hillel's view is followed. In Hebrew letters, fifteen is written tet vav, which sounds like tu. So: Tu BiShvat, the fifteenth of Shevat. It began as a date for bookkeeping. The Torah has rules about fruit trees, how a tree's first years of fruit are left alone, and which year's produce is tithed, so you need a birthday to count a tree's age. Mid-winter in the land of Israel is when the rains have mostly fallen and the sap is starting to rise. The almond trees are the first to blossom. Over time, the bookkeeping date turned into a celebration. Later, Jewish mystics in the tradition of Safed created a Tu BiShvat seder, a meal of fruits and nuts eaten in a special order, with cups of wine going from white to red, like winter turning to spring. Many people eat from the fruits the Torah praises in the land of Israel: "a land of wheat and barley, and vines and fig-trees and pomegranates; a land of olive-trees and honey," honey meaning dates. In modern Israel and around the world, it's also a day for planting trees and for thinking about the earth. The Torah even forbids cutting down fruit trees during a siege, asking: "for is the tree of the field man?" A tree can't run away. It's in your care.
screen: `FOUR NEW YEARS, ONE FOR TREES.` · `TU: THE FIFTEENTH OF SHEVAT.` · `THE SAP RISES, THE ALMONDS BLOOM.` · `FRUITS OF THE LAND, AND PLANTING.` · then, large: `FOR IS THE TREE OF THE FIELD MAN?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: eat a fruit and thank the tree. If you have one nearby, hold it now. Settle, and breathe. Look at it. Think of the tree it came from, the years it took to grow, the rain, the person who picked it. Taste it slowly. If you say blessings, Jews say one over tree fruit, thanking God who creates the fruit of the tree. Then think of one thing you're planting that you may never see finished. The bell holds the time.
Tu BiShvat. The fifteenth of Shevat: the new year for trees, marked with fruit, planting and thanks.
Your line: a birthday for trees. Today, stop at one tree and notice it, as if it were someone's birthday. Day one hundred thirty-two.

133.title: Purim: Esther
133.hook: a queen, a villain and a hidden God whose name never appears in the book
133.howItsDone: On Purim, Jews hear the book of Esther read aloud from a handwritten scroll, the megillah, both in the evening and again the next morning, often in costume.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tu BiShvat, the new year for trees. Your line was a birthday for trees. Did you stop at one? Now, a month or so later, the happiest day on the calendar. Day one hundred thirty-three.

Here's a story with everything. A king of Persia who throws a party for half a year. A queen who refuses his summons and is sent away. A beauty contest across the empire, won by a young Jewish woman who keeps her background secret, on her cousin's advice. A proud official who demands everyone bow to him, and when one Jew won't, plots to wipe out every Jew in the kingdom, and casts lots to pick the day. A sleepless king, a banquet, a sudden reversal. It reads like a palace thriller. And in the whole book, one name never appears.

segments.voice: The book is Esther, and on Purim it's read aloud from a handwritten scroll called the megillah. Megillah just means scroll, from a root meaning to roll. Purim means lots, the lots Haman cast to choose the day of destruction. And the name that never appears is God's. Not once, in the whole book. There are no miracles, no prophets, no voice from heaven. There's a queen who has to decide whether to risk her life by walking in to the king uninvited, and a cousin, Mordecai, who tells her that if she stays silent, help will come from somewhere else, and adds: "who knoweth whether thou art not come to royal estate for such a time as this?" She goes in. Everything turns. The rabbis loved this. They noticed that the name Esther sounds like the Hebrew for hidden, and they linked her to a verse in Deuteronomy where God says: "And I will surely hide My face in that day." So the book of Esther becomes the story of a hidden God. Not absent, hidden. Working through coincidences, a king's insomnia, a brave woman's choice. Many Jews say this is what most of life feels like: no parted seas, just timing and courage, and, if you look back, a pattern. It's also why Purim is so wild. People wear costumes and masks, hiding who they are, the way God is hidden in the story. And look at this week: a hut of branches, four kinds bound together, dancing with the scrolls, lights in the window, a count going up, a tree's birthday, and now a hidden name.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for help that doesn't announce itself. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last year. Was there a moment where something turned out right, and at the time it just looked like luck? A call at the right moment. A stranger. A delay that saved you. Pick one. Replay it slowly. You don't have to decide what it was. Just notice that it was there. The bell holds the time.
Megillah. A scroll, and on Purim, the scroll of Esther, read aloud: a story where God's name never appears.
Your line: hidden, not absent. Today, when something small goes right, pause and wonder who or what was behind it. Day one hundred thirty-three.
